Palm-leaf manuscript in Newari script;
*Samvarodayānāma Maṇḍalopāyikā* by Bhūvācārya at Ratnagiri.
In the year *a-cū-pteti-ghra* [174 = 1054 CE; 176 = 1056 CE according to Petech; 178 according to Matsunami], on the fourth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
Written during the reign of the King of Kings, Lord of Lords, Supreme Sovereign, the illustrious Baladeva Vijayarāja.
[Bhuvamati (Bhu ba blo ldan)—
see immediately below under Bhuvaripa (his teacher).]
— *The Collected Works* of the First Paṇchen Lama, vol. 2, p. 320.5.
Bhuvaripa — Templeman, *SIL*, p. 44.
— Templeman, TLK, p. 77 (and his student Bhuva Blo ldan, Bhuvamati?), p. 141 n. 232 (the lineage descending to him from Kṛṣṇācārya).
= Madhyadeśikamati (Dbus pa blo ldan)
The Ritual Manual for the Maṇḍala Entitled *Cakrasamvarodaya* (The Emergence of the Glorious Cakrasaṃvara).
Toh. no. 1538. Derge Tanjur, vol. ZA, folios 117v.2–150r.5.
— A worthy contender for the worst Tibetan translation ever:
*Ariṣṭadhīmat* (Dbu ba Blo ldan pa),
*Śrīcakrasaṃvarodaya-nāma-maṇḍalopāyikā*.
Ōta. No. 2249. Peking Tanjur, vol. 52, Rgyud 'grel XIV.
Quote: *Oṃ namaḥ śrīherukavajrāya*.
The verse states:
"With a mind purified by drinking the single flavor of the nectar of yoga..."

I always salute with my head that excellent and venerable Guru, whose body is purified by visiting sacred sites such as the *pīṭhas*, and who is the Lord of the mandala-circle of the supreme and glorious central *pīṭha*. || 1 ||
Now begins the great statement starting with "atha" and so forth, which concludes this tantra.
I pay homage to that Vajravārāhī, the sovereign of Cakrasaṃvara. || 2 ||
Verse by verse,
her body is adorned with a garland of goddesses who are jewels.
I always pay homage to her whose every limb is eternally conquered by heroes, who dwells in the center of the wheel, who is innate and stainless, and who is the essence of the yoga of Saṃvara. (3)
In the excellent interior of the lotus, which is the abode of the semen whose essence has the form of the letter E;
In the midst of that, white as a noble swan,
the perfected essence of all, omniscient, the abode of the utterly pure Buddha, the beautiful dwelling of the Goddess—
I pay homage to the Leader, Śrī Saṃvara, the innate and stainless one, the supreme delight. (4)
Verse by verse,
in the abode of the supreme mountain called Śrīratna, which is the very nature of the Vajra-mind.
Abiding there, I cry out in the assembly known as the *Saṃvara*, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of myself and others;

because of the arising of manifold emanations within the single dwelling of heroes, [I do so] in this form of sound in the midst of the circle of great yogins who possess many excellent qualities. (5)
Having bowed to the Lord of Vajra Conduct, who is the innate, incomparable essence of the mind alone;
Having offered my entire body at the feet of Vārāhī, the Vajra Goddess, and the excellent Guru... (2r)...
I shall describe this procedure for drawing the maṇḍalas, whatever little I have obtained.
Whether it be pure or impure, I do not know; yet I shall speak it constantly for the sake of generating happiness in one's own mind. (6)
The birth of the hairs on the body is like that of the sprouts of durva grass.

Just as iron immediately begins to revolve upon encountering a magnet, so too does this jewel of yoga shine within the hearts of those who apply themselves with diligence, attaining a state of redness through the substance of the powder of the night-blooming flower. || 7 ||
Furthermore, whatever is seen here in this text as being deficient in its verses, [it is because] it was abundant.
This is not an offense against my gurus; it is solely a fault of my own intellect.
And that which is both separate and combined, verse by verse;
Having understood the forward and reverse grasping in this tantra through the instruction of the guru,
I write it here for the sake of my own memory. (9)
The yogi whose essence is the welfare of others.
Endowed with both the conceivable and inconceivable natures,
the wise one, with a blossoming countenance,
eternally produces the flavor of existence and peace. 10.
Verse by verse:
first, the offering of water, the headband, the turban, and the vajra.

The empowerment of knowledge (vidyā-abhiṣeka) is named "the womb produced by the dominant [influence]," while the secret [empowerment] is "produced by excellent pleasure. Furthermore, there occurs at the end the empowerment of the consort's wisdom (jñāna-seka), which is designated as "the prophecy of having performed [the rites]. || 11 ||
In the wheel called Saṃvara, which has been composed with fixed rules for the purpose of accomplishing spiritual success.
If on the eighth day of the dark fortnight there occurs a favorable, black, empty, or full lunar mansion,
then having performed worship at night and having saluted the feet of the excellent Guru and the Hero,
the Pure Sole Hero should indeed undertake the commencement there for the benefit of all people. 12.
And as it has been said:
Who is capable of correctly delineating the mandalas according to reality?
Through union with one's own presiding deity, the construction of the mandala is perfected.
The mantra-practitioner should write each verse for the sake of accomplishment; if urged by a disciple, he should write them for the sake of merit.
Otherwise, one who seeks the substantial reality would not achieve it even in ten million births.
In each verse,
the worship of the mandala and so forth are taught for the sake of the co-emergent (sahaja).
The mandala of the Cakrasaṃvara Tantra is not to be drawn at all. 15.
Having undertaken the Saṃvaramaṇḍala for the sake of accomplishing each verse, it should be drawn.
Even by me it has been said that [the secondary] is never at all primary. (16)
One who has well contemplated the innate nature, who is skilled in devotion to the yoginīs, and who possesses the verses.

One who has departed from all delusion and is liberated from all evils, for whom there is no conceptualization regarding lunar days or religious observances— he will surely attain here the supreme enlightenment of the vow. (17)
Verse by verse,
one whose mind is focused on its own mental continuum should be engaged in the drawing of the mandala.

Having known all secrets, he is the sole master of all yoga; his mind is focused, he maintains the yoga of the heart, and being one who realizes the true nature of things through the *cchomaka* signs, that yogi, pure in mind and full of aesthetic vitality, writes with composure. 18.
Thereafter, having recited one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rule a single mantra-object, |||
The heart-mantra is likewise proclaimed as seven syllables,
together with the [mantra] of Karuṇakaravṛnda; by chanting it ten thousand times with fixed discipline, one destroys the deeds of Māra for the sake of the Vīras and Vīreśvarīs.
Having attained satisfaction in his own mind and the command of Heruka, verse by verse.
In the wheel produced by the innate (*sahaja*), he is instructed in the field (*kṣetra*).
He becomes a firm yogin, skilled in drawing the mandala;
indeed, he is not here one who is conceited or whose mind has a greedy disposition. (20)
Verse by verse,
that which has come down from the glorious pīṭha of Oḍiyāna through the succession of the guru’s oral instructions.
Indeed, for the sake of encouraging myself, I speak all this truth. (21)
Just as there is sweetness in molasses and heat in fire, so too is it with the verses.
In the same way, the bliss of the knowledge of the Goddess Mahāvīra is established. || 22 ||
And his activities are performed by the bhūtas, stationed in the form of a mandala.
The body is said to be the maṇḍala, as indeed is the powder maṇḍala.
As long as the body is free from disease, the wise person should undertake [the practice].
First, for the sake of accomplishing the two maṇḍalas, there is the worship according to the Dhairuka.
Verse by verse,
in the beginning of a great battle, when things have become deformed and exceedingly terrible.

Indeed, one should perform the preliminary service (*pūrvassevā*) in a cremation ground that is terrifying with the clamor of throngs of female *pretas*, and filled with *bhūtas*, *piśācīs*, and the wives of *śivas*. (25)
Verse by verse,
his mind was moistened with compassion fixed upon wisdom.
Satisfied by the method of tasting the nectar of yoga,
and having brought the three worlds under his power through loving-kindness and virtuous conduct,
he should undertake the practice for the sake of accomplishing the maṇḍala. || 27 ||
Whatever has been spoken or left unsaid in these verses, all that resides within Heruka.
Having reflected upon this purpose, it was adopted at the beginning of the community and so forth. || 28 ||
Verse by verse,
one should visualize the Guru’s pair of excellent sandals situated upon the crown of the head.
Having performed the placement of the seats (pīṭha) and so forth, one should begin the worship. || 29 ||
Having stepped with the left foot upon the right, with feet firmly placed, he is seated in the vajraparyaṅka posture.

Having meditated on the one of wrathful form, who has previously established the enclosure of stakes and the cage of the well-known ten directions, who holds a *ḍamaru* drum in one hand and a vajra-khaṭvāṅga in the other, and whose body is perfectly fashioned from all the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and so forth— one should visualize the Jewel Wheel (*cakraratna*). 30.
Verse quotation: Oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha hūṃ 2 phaṭ || Mantra 1 ||
Oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. Mantra 2.
Gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. (Mantra 3)
Oṃ ānaya ho bhagavān vajra huṃ huṃ phaṭ. (Mantra 4)
Form is that which is called Vairocana, and sensation perpetually arises as Vajrasūrya.

One should first cultivate the sense of "I" with true pride, thinking: "My perception (*saṃjñā*) is the illustrious Vajranṛtya, a treasury of diverse qualities; in Sanskrit, he is Vajrarāja. My consciousness (*vijñāna*) is Vajrasattva, the essence of the accumulation of forms consisting of all the Victors. Indeed, I am He-ka-ra-vajra. (31)
The eye is Śrīmohavajra, whose mind is innate bliss; in the two ears is Dveṣavajra.
In the nose is the Vajra named Envy; in the mouth is Passion-Vajra, who generates excellent beings.

In touch is Avarice-Vajra, conjoined with the object of sense; likewise, in the purification of the elements, he is thus well-established in all forms, producing supreme bliss and sporting in the net of Yoginīs. (32)
Verse by verse,
the goddess named Pṛthvīśrīlocanā, who manifests compassion and brings [beings] down, is the deity called Pātanī.

In the water element is Māraṇī, who, born from the Vajra family, is Bhūṣaṇā and possesses a mind of loving-kindness; in fire is Ākarṣaṇī, who carries the most intense heat; and in wind is Narteśvarī. In space is Padmaraśmī, who brings about all happiness and has the nature of the Dharmadhātu.
Verse by verse, through the purification of mindfulness of the body.
The *ḍākinī* is always accompanied by the liquid element;
*lāmā* is sensation and perception, and *tārā* has the nature of wind. (34)
Verses on the practice of recollection of the Dharma.
Janmaruhā is named Khaṇḍarohā;
she who is the form of the recollection of mind (cittānusmṛti) is Rūpavatī, known as Locanā. (35)
Cchandapracaṇḍā is verse by verse; Caṇḍākṣī possesses the miraculous power of vigor.
Prabhāvatī, Mīmāṃsā, Mahānāsā, and Cittagā. (36)
The verse states that Vīramatī is the faculty of faith.
Vīryendriya is said to be Kharvarikā; the one called Laṅkā is Smṛti; and Samādhi is known as Drumacchāyā. 37.
This great goddess, Ai+itī, is born from the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya).
And by means of these five faculties, the goddesses are proclaimed as being identical with them. || 38 ||
Verse by verse,
she is born of faith, most formidable, born of the vigor of wind, and born of heroism.
Surābhakṣī is Smṛti; Śyāmādevī is born from samādhi. || 39 ||
Prajñābalā and Subhadrā are said to consist of the five powers.
Hayā should be in the limb of concentration (samādhi), and Khagānanā in the limb of vigor (vīrya).
Cakravegā is always joyful, and Khaṇḍarohikā is serene.
Śauṇḍinī is indeed Dharmāṅgā, and Cakravarmiṇī is Smṛtyaṅgā. || 41 ||
Equanimity is the limb of heroism, and the seven factors of enlightenment are proclaimed.
Constantly endowed with these factors, the yogi sports upon the surface of the earth. || 42 ||
Verse by verse,
she is endowed with the great power of right view; she is the total consumer of conceptual thought.
Always pure in her conduct through right discipline, intent on the welfare of others, and skilled in accomplishing the aims of sentient beings;
always possessing great vigor and beautiful compositions of most diverse and eloquent speech;
and virtuous through the prowess of right action—she is indeed named Kākāsyā. (43)
Verse by verse,
you are the excellent protector of right livelihood, and you are daily known by the name of an owl.

The goddess Śvānāsyā always possesses a body formed for the thorough conquest of the afflictions; the one named Kolāsyā, however, has a beautiful form through the application of right mindfulness. All these goddesses possess the excellence of all aspects and are skilled in their respective activities. (44)
Indeed, Yamadrāḍī brings about the production of unreal merit for each and every verse.
For the protection of merit already produced, Yamadūtī is always considered [the presiding deity]. (45)
This verse is proclaimed as Yamadaṃṣṭrī for the destruction of unborn sins.
The Yamathanī is proclaimed for the purpose of destroying the sins already committed. || 46 ||
There are four types of desire. || 47 ||
The illustrious Vārāhī is perfectly established in the form of equanimity and meditative concentration.
And thirty-six awakenings (bodhayaḥ) have arisen from him as his limbs. || 48 ||
In each verse-quarter,
one should visualize the Lord Khaṇḍakāpālin at the place of his claws and teeth.
In the first [stage], he creates a great hero-skeleton at the end;
and from the hair of his hands, he produces the Siddha-skeleton-hero; and from the skin, through the purification of impurities, he creates the flesh-born Bhīmadraṃṣṭra. 49.
Verse after verse,
with sinews hardened by incomparable aesthetic flavor, [he] intoxicates Indra.
One should meditate on Amitābha, born from the bones of the one of immeasurable qualities and splendor;
and when the mind is prepared, one should contemplate the form of Vajratejas as the Vajra-body in the region of the stainless heart. 50.
One should place Aṅkurīka in the eyes, and Vajrajaṭa resides in the bile.
The great hero Phuphuśīka is adorned with the syllable HŪṂ in the intestines. || 51 ||
The *subhadra* mantra is at the base of the arms, and the *vajraśobhana* is in the abdomen.
And Bhairava in the region of the anus, with Akṣa beautifying the boundary. || 52 ||
In the case of phlegm,
[one should worship] the very powerful hero Ratnavajra; in the case of one's own pus, [one should worship] Mahābala.
And in the red [mandala], one should worship Hayagrīva, Viyadgarbha, and Svedadharmaja. || 53 ||
In each and every verse,
one should visualize the deity Śrī Heruka as Padmanartaka with tears.
In the phlegm [is] the Lord Vairocana, born from the *Ādibuddha* through the nasal mucus and so forth. || 54 ||
The heroes are declared to abide in the stable [vowels], while the yoginīs reside in the mobile [consonants].
Through the union of these two alone, the limbs of Heruka and his consort are said to be joined. || 55 ||
Having meditated upon the Lord Vajra-Hūṃkāra, who is fixed within beautiful rays of light at the end of the heart-lotus;

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to rule upon the six limbs—the heart, the top of the head, the tuft of hair, the shoulders, the two regions [of the arms], and the eyes—using stakes and other implements that possess the spreading radiance of lightning like a thunderbolt.
This incomparable, blazing splendor of the one named Saṃvara has thus been described. (56)
The first is Vairocana himself, and [the second is] the great Īśvara.
Heruka and Vajrasūrya are joined with the six-limbed horse. || 58 ||
Verse quotation: Oṃ haḥ | Namaḥ hi | Svāhā hu | Vauṣaṭ he | Hūṃ hūṃ ho | Phaṭ haṃ || Mantra 5 ||
At the navel is the goddess Vārāhī; she who is placed in the heart is Jvālamālā, the Night.
In the mouth is that Mohinī; on the head is the goddess named Surucitā-cālinī.
In the middle of the aperture of the crest-tuft is Santrāsī, of terrifying form, resembling blazing fire.
Caṇḍī has her excellent body fashioned over all parts of the limbs, her form being the armor of the mantra. (59)
Verse quotation: Oṃ baṃ | Hoṃ yoṃ | Hrīṃ moṃ | Hreṃ hrīṃ | Hūṃ hūṃ | Phaṭ phaṭ || Mantra 6 ||
The four essential mantras have as their intrinsic nature the mind of innate, perpetual bliss;
they are the singular essence of all forms, resembling a dense mass of radiance, and are the playful manifestation of the *ḍākinī* network.

Those qualities produced by sages, free from conceptual construction and its absence, well-established in that which is called restraint (saṃvara), should be meditated upon by the wise in the openings of the excellent vajra at the navel, heart, and head. (60)
Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye vajravarṇanīye huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā || Mantra 7 ||
Oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. || Mantra 8 ||
oṃ hrīḥ ha ha huṃ huṃ phaṭ || Mantra 9 ||
Oṃ śrī vajra he he ru ru kaṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ || Mantra 10 ||
Ḍākinījālasamvaraṃ svāhā. Mantra 11.
Ḍākinī is in the eastern face, while Lāmā resides in the beautiful left face;
Khaṇḍarohā is indeed in the rear face, and Rūpiṇī is in the southern face.

Those four skull-bowls, which possess both unitary and manifold natures, which produce supreme bliss, whose essential form is permanence and so forth, which are composed of nectar, which arise from emptiness, which are variegated,
whose sole essence is all-bliss, and which are the progenitors of the beings of the three worlds— [reside] within the corner of the lotus filaments.
These too, who are the sole heroes of all Buddhas, naturally well-born, should always be placed [therein]. || 62 ||
Pu is Pracaṇḍā Kāpālī, who resides in the aperture of the crest; Mahākaṅkāla, Caṇḍākṣī, and she well-known as Jālandhara [are likewise]. (63)
The letter *kā* is in the right ear, known as Oḍiyāna; it is Prabhāvatī together with Kaṅkāla. The letter *a* is situated in Arbuda. (64)
With formidable fangs and a large nose, she is stationed upon the backbone;
the arrangement of her [syllables] has been taught as it stands in the *Saṃvara*. 65.
The syllable *go* is in the left ear, known as Godāvarī;
joined with Vīramatī, it is well-established as Surāvairī. (66)
In the region between the eyebrows, at the place of Rāma, the syllable RĀ is situated;
she is conjoined with Amitābha, and is Kharvarī, whose form is fierce.
The great hero Vajraprabha, joined with Laṅkeśvarī, was stationed in Devikoṭṭa, the region of Dekāracakṣus. (68)
The letter MĀ is located at the base of the arm, well-situated in the place called Mālava;
this is proclaimed as the secondary seat (upapīṭha) known as Vajradehadrumacchāyā. (66)
By the very nature of the mind-wheel, the heroes and heroines abide;
this is declared in the Śrī Cakrasaṃvara to be the wheel named Khecarī. (67)
Kā resides in Kāmarūpa,
while the great hero Aṅkurika, accompanied by Airāvatī, is established between the two armpits.
The syllable O is in the region of the breasts, while in Oḍra the Vajrajaṭā resides;
joined with Mahābhairavī, it is designated by the name of the field (kṣetra). || 69 ||
The three syllables are always situated in the region of the navel within the Triśakunī;
she is joined with Mahāvīra, possesses the speed of wind, and is beautiful in form. (7v = 7l) 70.
The syllable *ko* at the tip of the nose, and the Vajra-hūṃkāra in Kośala, joined with Surābhakṣī, is proclaimed as being in the *upakṣetra*. || 71 ||
The letter *ka* is located in the region of the mouth, accompanied by Śyāmādevī; he is truly named Subhadra, a bearer of vows in Kaliṅga. (72)
The ornament at the region of the throat is celebrated by the name Lampāka;
Vajrabhadra is endowed with Subhadrā through the chandoha. || 73 ||
Having placed Kāṅkṣarā in the heart, Kāñcideśā is prescribed;
she is joined with Mahābhairava and is Hayakarṇā, the terrifying one. (74)
Indeed, Mṛḍhra is the one with great radiance and deformed eyes on Himālaya;
he is proclaimed by Upacchandoha and is joined with Khagāsyā. 75.
In the wheel of speech (vākcakra) is the goddess Bhūcarī, beautifully smiling and united with the hero;
she eternally bestows all accomplishments and abides in innate bliss. 76.
The Yoginī Cakravegā, endowed with great power, resides in the region of Vajra within the city of the Pretas. 77.
The syllable *gr* is located in the region of the anus, conjoined with the deity of the house;
Khaṇḍarohā, however, is well-established in the Melāpaka with Ratna.
The neck together with the region of the thighs,
accompanied by the goddess Śauṇḍinī and joined with its own syllable.
And know, O Vajra, that [it is] in Saurāṣṭra. || 79 ||
The syllable *sv* is in the shanks; by name she is Cakravarmiṇī, joined with Śagarbha, and she resides in the region of Hemabhū. (80)
The hero Sopamelāpaka is the letter Na, positioned on the finger;
Heruka is joined with the goddess Suvīrā in the city. (81)
Padmanarteśvara is situated on the back of a peacock, accompanied by Mahābala, in the cremation ground of the Sindhudeśa region. 82.
The letter Ma is in the region of the thumb; Vairocana resides in Maru.
He bestows all accomplishments, and his beloved is indeed Cakravartinī. (83)
One should place the syllable *ku* at the region of the knees;
one should always meditate upon Vajrasattva, conjoined with great heroism. (84)
The goddess who moves in the netherworld (pātāla) is established in the wheel of the body (kāyacakra).
The placement (nyāsa) in the three wheels has been taught as abiding both externally and internally. 85.
In the eastern direction and the others, one should place the heroes named Vajrasattva and so forth, seated upon lotus-sun cushions and adorned by yoginīs. (86)

The ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) has been fully described according to the tradition of the other teacher; having adopted whichever of these two is preferred, one should begin the practice. 87.
When the seed is in every respect united with the drop (bindu), then it is known as the fruit; so say the excellent yogins. (88)
Since the *bindu* is omnipresent, when it becomes marked by the syllable (*akṣara*), then bliss (*ānanda*) is attained; from bliss, the innate (*sahaja*) arises. (89)
The world arises from the coemergent; thus, arising would be coemergent.
However, the distinction between coemergence and arising has been described by me only in terms of conventional reality.
The goddesses with the faces of a crow and an owl, and those with the faces of a dog and a boar—this is declared to be the arrangement of the faces for the purification of the four faces. (91)
One should meditate upon Yamadāḍhī, Yamadūtī, and likewise Yamadraṃṣṭrī,
joined with Yamamanthānī, as situated in the corners.
Pure in the ten perfections, established on the ten stages, his self-nature consists of the ten cognitions, and he is established through tenfold divisions. || 93 ||
The stage Pramuditā (the Joyous), which follows the perfection of generosity, is on the seat (pīṭha);
while Vimalā (the Stainless), associated with ethical discipline, is proclaimed to be on the secondary seat (upapīṭha). 94.
In the [stage] Kṣetra, it should be known as Prabhākarī, which follows the perfection of patience; in the Upakṣetra, it is endowed with the Arciṣmatī, accompanied by vigor. 95.
In Cchandoha, she who is joined with meditation and stands on the ground of Abhimukhī is the Wisdom born of Upacchandoha, named Sudurjayā.
In the primary means of union (melāpaka), Dhātrī is always present;
in the secondary union (upamelāpaka), Acalā is eternally established in power.
They call the cremation ground the "vow"; it is always the stage known as Sādhumatī.
There, the Great King Śrī Heruka dwells and sports. 98.
The Self-Existent One, the Supreme Lord, is endowed with all supreme qualities;
he is the glorious abode of all heroes, whose single characteristic is his manifold forms. (99)
The stage of the Cloud of Dharma is proclaimed as always supreme in wisdom;
it is the abode of those who have previously been born [in the higher realms].
And the protection of Heruka has been taught by me. || 100 ||
On the *pīṭha* is suffering and ignorance; on the *upapīṭha*, origination;
on the *kṣetra*, the notion of cessation; and on the *upakṣetra*, the path is always present. (101)
In the Cchandohe [Tantra], there is the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) and the attainment of the desire for non-arising;
likewise, the assembly of the Dharma and its subsequent minor assembly. 102.
In the cremation ground is the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); in the *upaśmaśānika* [ground] is the knowledge of others' thoughts.
The purification of the seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth is said to consist of the nature of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*). (103)
In the Lakṣmī-gambhīra-sūtra as well, the gnoses are proclaimed;
they abide within the Cakrasaṃvara as the intrinsic nature of the Buddha’s form. (104)

One should visualize the goddesses and all the heroes in Pullīramalaya and the other sites, endowed with the arms that will be described hereafter, and possessing their respective colors and ages. (105)
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the yoginīs by virtue of their purity;
because they are joined through the placement upon the limbs, that is known as the Great Armor (Mahākavaca). || 106 ||
This, when joined with yoga, becomes another innate [state], endowed with both the external and the internal, and established as a limb of Heruka. || 107 ||
Because its intrinsic nature is unarisen, it is designated as "empty";
because it is the cause of dissociation, it is called "signless. (108)
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness. Mantra 12.

First, one should visualize emptiness; thereafter, having meditated upon the fire in the center of the syllable *vaḥ*, which has the form of excellent bliss, one should again generate the form of Indra’s vajra-sprout, which is the abode of water. Above that, one should fashion the celestial palace (*vimāna*), which is the best of mountains, possessing eight peaks and adorned with vajras.
It was uniquely beautified by various flowers and uniquely adorned with many diverse, great celestial garments. || 109 ||
It is endowed with bells and auspicious signs, making the quarters resound;
it is circular in shape, beautiful in its center with an excellent triple-layered enclosure adorned with garlands of flowers;
and on the outside, it has four gates beautifully fashioned with four great archways (*toraṇa*).
In the center, situated upon a universal lotus, is the formidable great blue vajra born of Bhava.
At its center is that which is called the *saṃvara*, endowed with the objects and commitments, having the nature of the five elements,
blue in form, possessing excellent splendor, fashioned by the pericarp, and consisting of the *hūṃ* born from the Lord Ananta; it is the Lord Heruka,
who has pervaded the limbs of Wisdom and reached all directions, and who is then withdrawn.
One should meditate upon the nature of an illusionist, who brings all existence to rest, in the center of a lotus.
The first excellent face has a smoky form and great brilliance; it is as beautiful as the crescent moon and possesses fangs.
The left face is dark blue, with a fine countenance and distorted, beautiful eyes; the face at the back is deep red.
The right face is golden-hued and most terrifying, abounding in boisterous laughter and the sound of "hi-hi."
The stainless one, who has overcome Śiva along with Durgā in the ālīḍha posture, and who sports with the host of ḍākinīs. 112.
His broad chest is adorned with a magnificent, expansive necklace woven from fifty severed heads;
his limbs are decorated with the six mudrās; his tawny hair is bound upward in a topknot by various human skulls;
the moon clings to the crest of that topknot; and his crown is marked by a universal vajra that has dispelled the darkness of the world.
He possesses a crest, joined thighs and arms, many tinkling bells, and a fierce vajra that resounds far and wide.
His broad elephant-hide, dripping with blood, is draped over his shoulder as a beautiful ornament;
in his right hands he holds a sharp trident, a boon-granting axe, a hand-drum, and a knife;
and in his left, a skull-topped staff, a lotus, a noose, and a severed head, which together adorn him as he conquers the three worlds.
One should manifest his form, which possesses every aspect, whose very nature is the pacification of all existence. || 114 ||

Threatening all the wicked, accompanied by a shower of thunderbolts, with disheveled hair and deep red in color, intent on embracing [the consort] by the neck, her mouth filled with blood, and holding a lotus in her left hand;
she is the nature of the mind of innate bliss and perpetual joy, through the single union of wisdom and means.
The Goddess Vārāhī appears like a dense cloud shimmering with infinite hosts of goddesses. 115.
With her cheeks dripping with blood that beautifies her entire body, she wears a garland of severed heads; naked and adorned with human bones.
And having encircled her husband’s beautiful thigh with her left shank, she brings joy to the hearts of yogins through her union with the essence of all wheels (cakras). 117.

One should visualize another woman with a monkey-like face, who is perpetually angry and characterized by our own [distinctive] manner of explanation; she has the form of a female face and is desired by both. 118.
Alternatively, one should meditate upon that Vajravārāhī, smoke-colored and characterized solely by universal bliss, as if she were another wish-fulfilling gem. (119)
The goddess who always resides in the center of the wheel through the yoga of churning is called Vajrakolāsyā; she is the leader who acts as the male.
The great goddess Vajraghoṇā, accompanied by all the goddesses,
should be meditated upon in her principal form for the sake of determining the meaning of the Samvara.
One should always meditate upon her wearing a tiger-skin garment, possessing three eyes,
and with her two feet busily moving with a distinct, gurgling sound.
Amidst the terrible cremation ground, filled with garlands of flames and as fearsome as Mahābhairava,
he sports in Sahaja as Sahajānanda Heruka.
One should meditate upon the Lord of the Wheel as being ever-present, kissing [the consort] with an embrace full of longing, by means of the Great Churning Yoga. 124.
Resembling the color of the moon, wrathful, with three eyes and a face turned to the right, and endowed with four fangs like hooks—this is proclaimed as the form for the western direction. 125.
With her right hand, the one of great splendor holds the formidable universal vajra that grants victory over the three worlds;
in her other left hand she holds a vessel filled with white and red blood.
Embracing him with both arms, Vajrahastā [holds] the bell that brings happiness to all people.
The goddess Vajravārāhī, who threatens [with her hand], whose essence is yoga, and who possesses innate bliss. 126.
One should meditate upon the ḍākinī known as Lāmā, who is Khaṇḍarohā and possesses a beautiful form, as she rejoices in the bliss of sexual union through the yoga of the vajra. 127.
The Yoginī is blue, dark, crimson-limbed, and yellow-hued;
she is beautiful with innate bliss upon the lotus petals in the four directions. (128)
There are four accomplished yoginīs situated externally and internally,
born from the states of the forms of water, wind, great fire, and earth.
Māmakī is the vow of loving-kindness, and Tāruṇī is the wisdom of equanimity; Pāṇḍarā is designated as strength, the cause of joyful prosperity.
Locanā is renowned as the skillful means, endowed indeed with compassion;
the purification of the ḍākinīs and so forth is said to have come down through the lineage of gurus. (131)
The Ḍākinīs and others are beautiful, dwelling in corpses, holding lotuses and khaṭvāṅgas in their hands;

with their right hands they hold flaying knives, and possess hand-drums; they have loose hair, three eyes, bodies adorned with the six mudrās, and are of a most terrible nature, appearing like fire with the heads of the best of men.
Standing in the ālīḍha posture, with mouths wide open, they utter the syllable *hūṃ* and are filled with the essence of bliss. || 132 ||
Alternatively, they may be well-seated upon tiger-skin garments;
endowed with the excellence of all forms, they should be meditated upon as bestowers of the accomplishment of all aims. 133.
In the directions starting from the southeast, proceeding clockwise through the east and south, and ending in the west,
one should contemplate the four-faced deity being kissed by his very faces according to their respective positions.
Having taken a Kṣatriya king together with his mother and father,
as well as another Kṣatriya, one should place a skull at the corner.
The fourfold worship is taught for the sake of purifying great delusion and the other afflictions;
it is declared in the Śrī Cakrasaṃvara for the purpose of worshipping the maṇḍala. (136)
Pracaṇḍā Khaṇḍakāpālī is situated on the southern spoke;
Mahākaṅkāla is in the east, accompanied by Caṇḍākṣī. || 137 ||
Kaṅkāla is in the northern region through his excellent union with Prabhāvatī;
Vikaṭadaṃṣṭra is in the west, accompanied by Mahānāsā. || 138 ||
Surāvairī, however, is well-united with Vīramatī in the southwest (nairṛtyā), while Amita and Kharvarī are always situated in the northwest (vāyavyā). || 139 ||
The goddess Vajraprabhā shall be the excellent one named Laṅkeśvarī;
she stands in the northeast, acting for the benefit of all sentient beings. (140)
In the southeast is Vajradeha, accompanied by Drumacchāyā;
these are said to be the Khecarīs of the mind-wheel in the Saṃvara. 141.
The exterior of the mind-wheel (cittacakra), however, is encircled by a row of blue vajras;
the heroes and the mistress of heroes are blue, joined with a radiating flood of Buddhas. 142.
One should place Aṅkurīka on the right, accompanied by Airāvatī;
Vajrajaṭila should be in the east, together with Bhairavī in her standing posture.
In the north, however, Mahāvīra is situated with Vāyuvegā;
in the west is Vajrahūṃkāra, accompanied by Surābhakṣī. || 144 ||
Subhadra is in the southwestern quarter, well-joined with the goddess Asyāmā; Vajrabhadra always resides in the northwestern quarter together with Subhadrā. (145)
Hayā is adorned in the northeastern direction at the site of Subhairava;
Khagāsyā, however, is in the southeastern direction, joined with Virūpākṣa. (146)
The Bhūcarī [wheel] is indeed the wheel of passion (rāgacakra), accompanied by a garland of lotuses;
it should always be meditated upon as red in color, performing the acts of emanation and withdrawal.
One should first place the jewel-vajra, which possesses great power, is always auspicious, is beautified by the speed of the wheel, and is delighted by Khaṇḍarohā. (148)
One should place Vājinī in the north, joined with Śauṇḍinī and Yoga; and one should place Ākāśā and Cakravarmiṇī in the abode of Varuṇa.
One should always meditate on Śrī Heruka and Suvīrā in the southwest, and on Mahābalā together with Padmanarteśvara in the northwest. 150.
One should always visualize the Great Delusion of the Cakravartin in the northeast;
one should contemplate Vajrasattva, the Great Hero, within the body wheel (kāyacakra). 151.
One should visualize a row of white wheels on the exterior as being white in color;
this is the characteristic of the conjunction with the underworld wheel (pātālacakra). || 152 ||
All the heroes are four-armed; they all hold a khaṭvāṅga in their left hands, while their right hands grasp ḍamaru drums; they are resplendent with their matted locks bound together. || 153 ||
But they, whose forms are throbbing with the nature of withdrawal, are well-seated upon corpse-thrones;
they are perfectly joined in the ālīḍha posture and adorned with bone garlands and other ornaments. 154.
Holding vajras and bells in their hands, they are intent on embracing the goddesses; they are naked in form, accompanied by the syllable *hūṃ*, and adorned with garlands of severed heads. || 155 ||
One should meditate upon the wheel of reality of innate bliss, the union of all heroes and yoginīs, which has emerged from that which is called the *samvara*. 156.
But those goddesses, beginning with Pracaṇḍā, are adorned by a single face;
they have two arms, loose hair, and are naked, yet adorned with human bones and the like. || 157 ||
In their left hands they hold red skull-cups, and in their right, the threatening gesture and flaying knives;
all are three-eyed, uttering the syllable *hūṃ*, and born from the nature of supreme bliss. (158)
The goddesses with girdles at their waists should be meditated upon with diligence;
they possess both singular and manifold natures, and are capable of consuming the blood of the wicked. 159.
The four goddesses, beginning with Ḍākinī, proceed in counter-clockwise order; because the world arises from the left, they are thus described in the Cakrasaṃvara. (160)
From the union of white and blue, smoke-colored [light] certainly arises;
because of its blueness, the Ḍākinī is said to be situated in front. (161)
Those with the faces of crows and owls, and likewise those with the faces of dogs and pigs—blue, dark-green, red, and yellowish in hue—are stationed at the gateway. (162)
In the southwest corner, one should always visualize Yamadāḍhī, who is supremely terrifying;
in the northwest, Suviśuddhā.
Yamadūtī and Cāruvastrā. || 163 ||
In the northeast is Yamadaṃṣṭrī,
whose nature is to take sole refuge in the left-handed conduct;
she is Yamamathanī, perfectly pure.
She should always be meditated upon in the place of fire. || 164 ||
This has been proclaimed for this purpose both in reverse order and in direct order;
in the Yogatantra there is no fixed sequence, whereas in the Yoginīkrama it is so described.
Possessing divine forms and great majesty, endowed with two colors, these excellent goddesses of the corners are the destroyers of obstacles in the world. (166)
In the left [hands] are a khaṭvāṅga and a lotus, and in the right, a ḍamaru and a knife;
stationed at the gates and other locations, these embrace Heruka and are full of passion. (167)

The wise one, having meditated upon the syllables beginning with *pu* at the head, crest, and other [limbs]—namely *pū*, *jā*, *o*, *a*, *go*, *rā*, *de*, *mā*, *kā*, *o*, *tri*, *ko*, *ka*, *laṃ*, *kā*, *hi*, *pre*, *gṛ*, *sau*, *su*, *na*, *siṃ*, *ma*, *ku*—[should perform the ritual]. 168.

Thereafter, one should invoke the Cakra, beautiful with innate bliss (sahajānanda), with its feet treading [upon the ground] and its gaze directed upward, while emitting the sound of "phetkāra" from the head. 169.
One should invoke the heroic yoginīs residing in the world-systems of the ten directions;
for all are innate bliss (sahajānanda) by virtue of being the form of the excellent means of happiness. 170.
One should carefully wrap it at the tip, and even when it has reached the middle, one should cause it to be done;
when the two [ends] have increased and are joined together, one should cause it to be done at the ends of the forehead.
When the yogin has thus been made to revolve, he, being joyful, should utter the mantra;
having empowered that which stands upon the excellent wheel through the purity of the tip of the vajra-lotus. (172)
Hoḥ || Mantra 13 ||
From the syllable *dyā*, the pericarp is born; from the syllable *vyā*, the vajra arises.
Having first performed the placement of the four limbs (*caturaṅganyāsa*), one should thereafter practice for bliss. || 173 ||
The Hero is primarily bliss, while the Yoginī is supreme bliss;
and all are innate blisses by virtue of being the means to true happiness. (174)
In this world of heaven, mortals, and so forth, one shall in an instant become the single embodiment of all bliss, as proclaimed in the *Cakrasaṃvara-saṃvara*. (175)
The Hero, endowed with non-duality,
whose nature is the deity manifesting as the form of the mind,
is a yogi established in vast compassion.
But the innate [state] resides in the center of the wheel. || 176 ||

Having fully worshipped the all-pervading Lord of the mandala with offerings both external and internal, one should do so through the purity of the threefold yoga by means of the non-apprehension of the giver and the rest. (177)
Wherever there is worship and praise, it is seen in all the tantras;
having reflected upon this purpose, I praise the Hero with a concentrated mind. (178)
You are the venerable Vajraḍāka, clinging to the neck of the supreme Yoginī;
your body possesses a wondrous form through the merit of the lineage of heroes.
You are the one whose power is the great compassion of Saṃvara abiding within the maṇḍala.
I ever worship your lotus-feet, O All-pervading Lord. || 179 ||
The crown-lock (jūṭa) is adorned with the King Akṣobhya and embellished with the flame-seal;
it is described as the abode of all Buddhas from the perspective of the ultimate meaning. 180.
According to the view of our Guru, the Universal Vajra is said to be upon the matted locks;
that very consecration is said to have come down through the sequence of the conduct-vow. (181)
In the great square wheel, the leader is Ratnasaṃbhava;
likewise, in the eight-petaled lotus wheel, there is Amoghasiddhi. (182)

The supreme goddesses, Kākā and the others, embraced by [the lords] Vajra, Aṅkuśa, and so forth, should be visualized as eight [goddesses] well-established upon corpses according to another tradition. (183)

The faces of these goddesses with crow-like mouths are depicted according to their names, as they have been handed down through the lineage of our Guru; for that reason, it has been written by him. (184)
Furthermore, there is the form of a woman's face and the faces of goddesses;
the knower of yoga should always take whichever he prefers from between these two. (185)
Mahākaṅkāla, Kaṅkāla, Hayagrīva, Śauṇḍinī, Khagāsyā, Hayakarṇī, and the others—these are to be visualized according to their names. 186.
The heroes are proclaimed as having various emanated forms of the Goddess;
these are to be visualized in the Śrīsaṃvara according to their literal descriptions and activities. (187)
That which begins with the basis of the aggregates and extends as far as worship and praise is called the "arising" of the initial yoga; it is designated as the "mild yoga. (188)

Upon the production of the seed-syllable situated on Mount Meru, one should perform the visualization of the mandala and so forth by means of the middle division; this is the characteristic of Atiyoga.
Awakening in a single moment is the characteristic of the penetration of gnosis;
the yogi who is always engaged in the great yoga is proclaimed as being of the highest degree. (190)
Established in this very Great Yoga, one should always practice the yoga of all things as auspicious, with an intensity exceeding the most intense. (191)
For all yoga has him as its foundation; he is reeling with innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), the glorious abode of all heroes, self-arisen, and the knower of all yoga. (192)
The characteristics of the consecrated site have been stated by the venerable Śrīdārikāpāda;
therefore, having propitiated the Guru, one should commence every yoga. (193)
He laughs, weeps, and dances most beautifully;
he is the creator of the universe, the omniscient of all, and as lovely as a web of yoginīs.
It is stated right here:
A man who is devoted, pure, a light-bringer, and virtuous. || 195 ||
One should first perform these factors of enlightenment, equipped with their own armor and joined with the great armor; once they are accomplished, however, one should abandon them.
Once accomplished, he performs the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the three syllables according to the prescribed rule;
its form is that of the three wheels, through the yoga of the purification of the three bodies.
The syllable Oṃ should be recited in the body wheel, while the prostration of the syllable Āḥ is performed;
having made the mental placement of the syllable Hūṃ, one should perform the recitation according to the ritual rule.
Arising from the power of conceptualization and having the welfare of sentient beings as its cause,
this placement of the three syllables is, through yoga, the very nature of reality.
And so it has been said:
"The body is the unarisen syllable; speech and mind are the imperishable. It is the non-conceptualized space-vajra, the gathering of false aggregations. (200)
All [mantras] are illuminated by the syllable *oṃ* and joined with *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*;
for the sake of accomplishing success (*siddhi*), one should begin the recitation (*jāpa*) according to their names. || 201 ||
Having recited the mantra of emptiness as well as that of Sumbharāja,
one should meditate upon a rampart and a cage, and likewise upon the ground as consisting of vajras.
The wind and fire circles, the water and Indra’s [earth] circle, the universal vajra, and Mount Sumeru together with the universal lotus. (16v = 16l) || 203 ||
Above that, produced from the eighty minor marks, is a moon mandala;
upon the moon-seat is the syllable HŪṂ, from which arises the maṇḍala of Heruka. (204)
Accompanied by Vārāhī and others, terrifying with various colors and forms, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, most formidable, and endowed with female gatekeepers. || 205 ||
One should personally meditate upon the Hero Samvara, who brings about all accomplishments and is endowed with the armor and great cuirass of the six heroic Yoginīs. (206)
Having first performed the placement of the three syllables, one should commence the recitation;
this is what is to be meditated upon in the Śrīsaṃvara, though other yogins describe it differently. (207)
For by whatever state the minds of men are joined, they attain the nature of that very thing, just as a crystal takes on the form of everything before it. o || 208 ||
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Lord of Heroes; huṃ huṃ phaṭ. (Mantra 14)
Oṃ, to the one resembling the fire at the end of a great eon, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Mantra 15.
Oṃ, to the one with fierce matted locks and a crown, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. (Mantra 16)
Oṃ, to the one with a terrifying face whose fangs are formidable at the tips, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! (Mantra 17)
Oṃ, to the one radiant with a thousand arms, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. Mantra 18.
Oṃ, to the one who wields the axe, the noose, the trident, and the khaṭvāṅga staff, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. (Mantra 19)
Oṃ, to the one wearing a tiger-skin garment, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. Mantra 20.
Oṃ, to the one whose body is great smoky darkness, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. (Mantra 21)

Oṃ kuru 2 huṃ huṃ phaṭ || Mantra 23 ||

Oṃ bhakṣa 2 huṃ huṃ phaṭ || Mantra 32 ||
Oṃ, to you who wear a garland of hanging flesh, blood, and entrails, seize, seize! Huṃ huṃ phaṭ! Mantra 33.
Oṃ, threaten the serpent-dragons dwelling in the seven netherworlds! Huṃ huṃ phaṭ! (Mantra 34)

The root mantras of the heroes (vīra) of Kāyaca[ka]:
[Oṃ]. Others say that the Lord of Heroes (Vīreśa) is proclaimed with "Kara" at the beginning;
according to our own Guru’s tradition, this is how the mantra of the heroes is spoken. [Oṃ] 209.

Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī, the Noble Invincible One! O Mother of the Three Worlds, O Knowledge-Mantra, O Bringer of Fear to all Beings, Great Vajra, Seated on the Vajra-Throne, Unconquered, Invincible, Enchantress, Whirler of Eyes, [Poison-]Drier, Wrathful One, Furious One, Terrifying One, Frightener, Slayer, Excellent Divider, Seizer, Victorious Over Defeat, Paralyzer, Stammerer, Deluder, Vajravārāhī, Great Yoginī, Mistress of Desire, Sky-Goer!
It is thus: Prot-aṅge 2! Strike 2! The vital breaths! Kiṃkiṇi! Khiṃkhini! Shake 2! O Vajra-Handed One! Dry up 2!

O bearer of the vajra, khaṭvāṅga, and skull-cup; O devourer of great flesh and meat; O you clothed in human entrails; O wearer of a garland of human heads strung together; O Śumbhanī-Śumbhe! Destroy, destroy the life-breaths of all sacrificial victims! O cutter of great flesh; O embodiment of wrath; O you with terrifying fangs; O Great Seal; O Chief Queen of the glorious Lord Heruka; O thousand-headed one, thousand-armed one, thousand-faced one; O you of blazing splendor; O Jvālāmukhī; O you with tawny eyes; O you of vajra-body; O you seated upon the vajra; O you who are joined and matted!

He he huṃ huṃ kha kha yu yu ka ka dhuru dhuru muru muru! O non-dual Great Yoginīs, perfected by recitation! Dreṃ dreṃ dhreṃ dhreṃ graṃ graṃ he he hā hā! O Terrible One, laugh, laugh! O Heroine, hā hā ho ho huṃ huṃ! O Destroyer of the Three Worlds, surrounded by a retinue of ten million billion Tathāgatas! Huṃ huṃ phaṭ! O you who have the form of a lion, khaḥ! O you who have the form of an elephant, jaḥ! O you whose belly is the three worlds, O you whose girdle is the ocean, swallow, swallow! Huṃ huṃ phaṭ!

O you who are non-dual from the Hero, *huṃ* + *hā* 2, O *Yogeśvarī* who deludes the great beast, you are the *Ḍākinī* of worldly beings; accept this *bali* immediately for me! *huṃ* *huṃ* *phaṭ*! O terrifier of spirits, O Great Heroine, O Supreme Accomplished One, O Mistress of Knowledge, *phaṭ* *huṃ* *huṃ* *phaṭ* *huṃ* *huṃ* *phaṭ* *svāhā*! (Mantra 47)

The yogi should recite these mantras, which are connected with the yoginīs and heroes, as well as others arising from the Saṃvara cycle, for the sake of attaining all desired goals and benefits. (210)
In the system of Indrabhūti, according to the tradition of the Dārikā school, the heroic deities are said to have two arms and one face. (211)
And according to the opinion of the venerable Jālandharapāda and Kacchapaṭṭi, the heroic Yoginīs are proclaimed to have one face and two arms. (212)
The ḍākinīs and others, together with the vīras and accompanied by the gatekeepers, are wrathful in form, endowed with the syllable hūṃ, having one face and four arms. || 213 ||
Likewise, the goddesses beginning with Pracaṇḍā have various colors in particular;
according to the system of Caryāpāda, they indeed possess two arms and one face. 214.
Alternatively, through the purity of mind,
they possess the form and single color of blue;
these heroes are joined with goddesses.
These were spoken according to the consensus of some. || 215 ||

Established through the threefold distinction of the purity of the three bodies (trikāya) and by means of the three colors, the triple wheel (tricakra) is taught; therefore, there are three colors. || 216 ||
Among these, O knower of yoga, practice devotion to whichever form you prefer, beginning from the two-armed form up to the one with a hundred thousand arms and faces. (217)
One should meditate through the yoga of the inconceivable for the sake of infinite accomplishment;
having understood this, the wise person should act, for deliberation is not appropriate. (218)
All this is indeed the supreme moon; for whatever is to be cultivated is the fruit of truth.
Having received the words of the Guru with a mind full of devotion, || 219 ||
Some teachers say that the Jvālāmudrā is indeed taught in the *Saṃvara*, yet it is stated in the *Herukābhyudaya-tantra* that it does not exist at all in the *Saṃvara*. 220.
It was not written by me; therefore, O Vajravīra, it should be forgiven.
Vārāhī has been proclaimed through the instruction of the flame-seal (jvālamudrā). 221.

Regarding the matter of clothing, it has been stated by the mantras of Vīreśa that even one wearing a tiger skin is [suitable]; furthermore, our Guru has taught that the innate garment of Vajraḍāka is the form of a corpse,
eternally smoke-colored and fierce, with a body of white blood, for the sake of the six lumps and the owl.
The goddess has a form identical to [that of] Varṇā and the others, with her hair loose and her face turned toward the first direction. 223.
Having observed these two views, one should produce that which creates an inclination in the heart;
for while another [view] holds that the right channel carries the blood of a menstruating woman more forcefully,

Marrow, bone, sinew, and water—these five, combined with the father's semen, come into being. || 224 ||

The skin, flesh, and blood of the mother, together with the subtle *nala*, these two are perfected; that Lord who generates this is Śrī Heruka, who is non-different from those generated by his parents.
In this [tantra] called Śrī Saṃvara, which is a treasury of all qualities and the intrinsic nature of all phenomena—

Śambhu, accompanied by Girijā. || 268 ||

Because all pride and the like have departed, it is called a "palace" (vimāna).

When passion has departed through the connection with the fourth moment, he who is endowed with the excellence of all aspects is called a Hero (vīra). || 273 ||
In that very place, she who has attained sovereignty, whose nature is emptiness and compassion,

Passion and the other afflictions are like chaff, consumed by the gnawing of gnosis;

In the sky, in the lotus, in the midst of the void, he is one whose nature is to delight in the wheel of the Khecarī;

Oṃ trāṃ hrīṃḥ khaṃ on the petals;

Mild, medium, intense, and intensely intense—these four distinctions of the mind produce transformations among humans and other beings. (289)

Bliss, supreme bliss, and the third, the cessation—this is the innate nature of all that is stable and moving. (295)

The reality of the self is eternally conjoined with the reality of the mantra-maṇḍala;

Through an object of focus one becomes a Buddha, but when without an object, one is the Vajra-holder.

It dissolves into all the limbs; this is the characteristic of the *saṃvara*.

It dissolves into the nature of the Dharmakāya; of this there is no doubt.

In these locations, bliss arises always according to reality;
having arisen, it persists and then gradually dissolves.
At the door of the nostrils (ghāṭana), there is the impelling of Vajraḍākinī;
at the apertures of Śrījālandhara, bliss arises at that very moment. (307)
The aggregate, consisting of the stable and the moving, arises through bliss;
that is Heruka together with Vārāhī, the Buddhas and so forth, joined with the heroes. (308)
The aggregates and so forth are the Buddhas; for those elements, there is the innate [nature], which has two aspects due to the conceptualization of female, male, and so on. (309)
All sense objects are said to be space, which is the immortal;
because she moves therein, she is considered the "Space-Moving Being" (Sattvākāśacarī).
The heart of the entire network of ḍākinīs is the supreme Saṃvara;
in this, there is neither rosary nor recitation, for it is innate, all-pervading, and ever-present. (311)
Therefore, having generated devotion through great effort with a mind free from conceptual construction,
one should always remain in the playful state of yoga, having abandoned fear and shame.
Herein [are described] the two excellent practices of recitation and fire-offering,
the sacrificial rite, the object of meditation, the mandala and so forth, as well as the ritual procedures for the vase and the colored powders and lines.
One should know that which is situated as the innate (sahaja) within the body. || 313 ||

having incinerated the Buddhas residing in the wheel of gnosis, she moves into the wheel of enjoyment. 315.
Having worshipped the means (upāya), she becomes situated within the treasury of the ūrṇā-hair;
then, having issued forth from the gateways of the vital points (marmadvāra) known as Oḍiyānaka, [she remains there]. 316.

she is like a water-wheel (*arahaṭṭaghaṭikā*) for the resting of the mind;

Remaining here, she goes forth and likewise returns;

Thereafter, the wise one, exerting himself in deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, should begin the mandala. || 322 ||
"She is the goddess of all Buddhas"—thus she is described in the *Dārikāmata*;
she is also mentioned in the *Herukābhyudaya* and other texts by Jālandhara and others. (323)
In accordance with the meaning of the oral tradition of the Samāja tantras, the mantra-practitioner should draw the Cakrasaṃvara maṇḍala for the sake of the vow (saṃvara). 324.
I shall describe the characteristics of the Ācārya as they are agreed upon in the Tantras as they have been taught:
in his left hand he holds a khaṭvāṅga, and in the other [right hand] he holds a ḍamaru while uttering the syllable HŪṂ. (325)

= *Herukābhidhāna* 2.4–5c (slight changes made here to rectify the meter: the Baroda manuscript reads *kapālakṛtamūrdhajaḥ | bhasmānuliptāṅgaḥ*; that is, what is here the sixth *pāda* is an odd *pāda* in the source text, therefore my emendation is justified; it is also supported by the Tibetan translation).

"The great guru was asked by that disciple regarding the worship and other rites: [verse].
With a joyful heart, he should say: "Everything has been accomplished by me. || 327 ||
[The text reads: *pṛṣṭo*, *pṛṣṭau* (perhaps itself a correction); *'sau*, *sau*.

This and the following verse describe the optimal scenario, wherein the initiate has personally arranged for the collection of all requisites necessary for the initiation. This motif is attested in other manuals; for example, in Kukkurāja’s *Sarvabuddhasamāyogamaṇḍalavidhi* (172v): "O son of noble family, do you possess the necessary resources?"
"State what necessary materials are available; if those that are incomplete can be obtained, they should be gathered when all things are in abundance.
All food, drink, and so forth, along with clothing and offerings, [should be prepared].
For the sake of worshiping the Vīradevīs, this was caused to be made by me according to the prescribed rite. || 328 ||
Then, moreover, here the Great Hero is non-dual, being perfectly united with the limb of wisdom.
The great yoga of Śrī Heruka is established within all the cakras. || 329 ||

Regarding the locations where the maṇḍala should be drawn according to the *Herukābhidhāna*, see verse 355 below. The expression *krodhayogataḥ* is somewhat opaque: it could simply mean that the officiant should adopt a wrathful state of mind (cf. *Ḍākinīvajrapañjaraṭippaṇī* Ms 7r).

"By means of the yoga of wrath" (*krodhayogena*) refers to the ego-sense of wrath (*krodhāhaṃkāreṇa*); however, it may also refer to something more specific, namely the visualization of oneself as a wrathful deity or a particular deity (cf. *Pradīpodyotana*, p. 165, which identifies Yamāntaka as the primary option). The "summoning mantra" (*ākṣepamantra*) consists of the set of four mantras beginning with *oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha* (see above, mantras 52–55); cf. [source].

*Ākṣepamantra*: the four-faced mantra beginning with *oṃ sumbha ni-sumbha*, etc. (*Cakrasamvarābhisamayaṭīkā* p. 169 ad *Cakrasamvarābhisamaya* v. 33). Regarding the phrase "well-guarded by the *ākṣepamantra*" (*Saṃcāratantranibandha* ad *Yoginīsaṃcāra* 15.10): one should perform protection continuously by reciting the four-faced mantra again and again.
[The verse continues:
"Having gathered disciples who are worthy and capable of practicing the *samvara*..."
Those who are engaged in the practices prescribed for the vows and are preceded by devotion to Vārāhī. || 332 ||
[One should select] those who desire merit, who are pure, skillful, and have reached the further shore of the drawing of mandalas.
One should also undertake [the practice] together with those who are contented and affectionate.
Verse! The two preceding verses appear to describe not the initiands themselves, but rather those disciples who have already received initiation and will assist the officiant in drawing the maṇḍala.

Having offered the bali sacrifice and other offerings, and having worshipped the heroic guru who abides as the non-dual Heruka, one should commence the purification of the ground.

Verse! The plural nominative *saṃsthitāḥ* appears to refer to both the preceptor (*ācārya*) and the chosen disciples, unless one is to emend it to *-saṃsthitaḥ* to accord with the singular optative *samārabhet*. Verse.
In mountain caves and groves, or on the shores of the great ocean,
or in a cremation ground that has been established from the beginning— one should draw the maṇḍala there.
Verse 1.15 of the *Herukābhidhāna*, a transcription by Sanderson of *JRY Yoginīsaṃcāra* 9.3. This verse appears in several other locations, where it is usually read as *ādisiddhaśmaśāne*.

There, one should smear the ground of the mandala with the cow-dung of a drinking cow, combined with cremation-ground ashes and endowed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). || 336 ||

Verse 2.1 of the *Herukābhidhāna*—which is a copy of JRY *Yoginīsaṃcāra* 9.4, as traced by Sanderson—occurs in other locations as well. Regarding the term *pānagomayena*, the Tibetan translation provides an interpretive rendering, *lci ba ma ltung bas*, corresponding to *apatitagomayena*. The editors of the *Herukābhidhāna* at Sarnath offer a similar reading, *apātagomayena*, though it lacks manuscript support.

The *Cakrasaṃvaravivṛti* (Sarnath ed. p. 28; Li Nan ed. p. 84) interprets *pānagomaya* as Vairocana, that is, semen (note that the Sarnath editors have adjusted the lemma). The non-standard, yet likely original, reading *-bhūmiṃ pralepayet* (or *-bhūmiṣu lepayet* in the *Abhidhānottara*) has here been grammatically, but not metrically, ameliorated.
The *Cakrasamvaravivṛti* (ibid. clarifies the causative form *upalepayet* by [stating] "the preceptor [causes] the disciple [to smear]" (*śiṣyeṇācāryaḥ*).
The verse reads:
"Then, having smeared the ground, one should begin the mandala there."
Having thoroughly kneaded and pounded the ground with water scented with perfumes using the medium or superior breath, one should diligently make the earth level and pure.
[On] the earth, [on] the earth... one should make it level. (ab = Herukābhidhāna 2.2ab;
cd = Herukābhidhāna 1.6ab; see notes to the following verse).

The verses beginning with "madhyamā" which have been spoken, along with their explanations based on wordplay (śleṣa), must be understood when the true Guru is satisfied; otherwise, they are not known at all. 338.
-gurau], -guru! This refers to 337c (= Herukābhidhāna 1.6a) cited above. For an extensive discussion of this passage, see Sanderson 2009: 212ff.

The original Śaiva reading in the *Brahmayāmala*/*Picumata* was almost certainly *madhyamottamacchāgena*, designating three types of sacrificial victims (cows, humans, and goats); however, this meaning was obscured in the Buddhist adaptation, likely due to a scribal error.
Bhūvācārya was undoubtedly aware of the exegetical difficulties associated with this scriptural passage and chooses instead to direct the reader toward oral instruction.
If the north and east are submerged, success always comes to practitioners of mantra;
if the center is elevated, there will be sovereignty and the ranks of the Vidyādharas. (339)
Success, success! [The word *siddhiḥ* is glossed with *bhavati* by a second hand in the lower margin.

This verse most likely originates from the *Vajraḍākatantra* 46.83; however, there is a curious contradiction here, as that scripture advocates the *madhyonnata* (center-elevated) type of ground as the best and describes the *pūrvonnata* (east-elevated) type as undesirable: "Success does not come for the practitioners of mantra on a site sloping toward the east or the north."

If the center is elevated, there will be sovereignty or the status of a *vidyādhara*. (Cf. Padmaśrīmitra’s *Maṇḍalopāyikā* 1.31: "The ground that is uneven—low or high—should be abandoned; one should accept ground sloping toward the northeast. If the center is elevated, there will be sovereignty or even the state of a *vidyādhara*.
If the north is elevated, there will be death or the loss of wealth.")
The destruction of the family will quickly come to pass, just as previously described in the section on the rising [of the asterisms]. (340)

Death would occur; there would be the loss of wealth, O Goddess, or else the onset of disease. There would quickly be the destruction of the family, just as was stated regarding the previous elevation. (Note: The word *d* is unmetrical because it is a scriptural quotation [see below]; this is very likely a slightly modified version of *Vajraḍākatantra* 46.84–85ab.)

A more standardized version appears in Padmaśrīmitra’s *Maṇḍalopāyikā* 1.32 (Ms 1v4–5): “If the ground is elevated toward the north, there will be death, or else the loss of wealth; the lineage will quickly perish if the ground is elevated toward the east.
If the ground is depressed in the center, the practitioner is destroyed.”
Thus the stage with its characteristics has been defined, beginning with Vīreśa and the others.

By means of the syllable *ma*, the right eye is made into the sun; by means of the syllable *ṭa*, the left eye is made into the moon.
