Possessing the six mudrās and joined palms, naked and with hair loose, the mudrā is as follows:
holding a *khaṭvāṅga* in the left hand and a *ḍamaru* in the right, which is sounded stainlessly;
having taken [the disciple] to the front, with the left thigh positioned between [the legs], the disciple is made to face the sky.
The supreme Guru, who is well-established in what is to be consumed and most excellent, shall fulfill the desires of the moon. 717.

Having abandoned the emanation, the yogin should take with his tongue that which is stainless in both respects; thereafter, with a smiling face, he should bestow the command upon the disciple situated at the crown of the head, saying:
"Take with your tongue this essence, produced by supreme passion, which rests within the lotus."
Afterwards, having taken his hand according to the prescribed rite, he should give that stainless Yoginī to him.
The yogi should take with his tongue that which has become free from conceptual elaboration and is stainless;
then, with a face fully blossomed upon his skull-cup, he should bestow the secret upon the disciple.
You must taste with your tongue the essence that arises as supreme bliss, abiding within the lotus.
Then, taking her by the hand, he should bestow that faultless yoginī upon him according to the ritual procedure. 718.
This goddess, who bestows accomplishment upon you and consists of the five elements and the five tastes, [is to be enjoyed] through the yoga of the nature of Śrī Heruka; partake of true bliss. (719)
This goddess bestows accomplishments; she is the essence of the five elements.
Through union with me, Heruka, bring bliss to perfect purification. 719

O child, having joyfully and firmly embraced the excellent lotus [of my heart], do not speak of what is expressible or inexpressible; experience that bliss which is the essence of the form of restraint (*saṃvara*).
As for everything else—such as the nature of great bliss produced by pleasure—that has already been explained.
Having understood this, perform thereafter whatever you desire, day and night, with the jewel of the reality of meditative cultivation.
Behold! Here in front, with joy, he firmly embraces the supreme Lotus-Born with delight;
that which is wordless and ineffable, the power of excellence, is the very essence of the nature of Saṃvara.
All others, as they have been taught, consist of the nature of joy arising from bliss and so forth.
Having understood this, one should thereafter act as one desires, while meditating day and night on that very jewel. 720.
The goddess, possessing the characteristics previously described, uttered this vajra-sound:
"O Hero, are you able to devour the one born from the lotus? (721)
Having clearly shown the characteristics of the goddess, Vajraghoṣa shall speak:
"O Hero, in what do you take delight? [I am] born from the lotus, and [desire] food. (721)
And those four joys, accompanied by the edible and the inedible—
by means of these, O perfectly awakened one who is undifferentiated, speak then of Heruka-vajra.
"O Heruka, tell me: what are these four joys, and is that [joy] also the indivisible, excellent intellect? Is it so? (722)
Then the disciple should also say: "I am always able to do it. Having opened her lotus-like face, she, being delighted, should speak to him whose mind is pure. (723)
Then the disciple shall also speak: "I am always able to perform [this];
with a joyful mind like a blooming lotus, I shall speak with a pure heart. (723)
O Padme, perform whatever duties are required, such as the propitiation of the vows and so forth;
always abandoning fear and shame, take delight in the supreme vow. (724)
O Padma, act as you have been instructed! Constantly behold the terrifying and the marvelous, such as the propitiation of Cakrasaṃvara; sport in the supreme bliss! 724.
Then the wise disciple performs all that which was thus prescribed:
[he visualizes himself] seated upon the thrones of the four Buddhas, well-established upon the vajra-lotus. (725)
Just as the Master has taught, all those of noble intelligence abide upon the seats of the four Buddhas, well-established on the vajra and lotus. 725
Having experienced in due order that which is characterized by the four joys, and having consumed their arising, he pays homage to the Guru and the Yoginīs. (726)
The characteristics of the four joys should be practiced in their proper sequence; thereafter, one should partake of excellent food and prostrate to the Guru and the Yoginī. 726.
One should perform the vajra-essence, the impetuous feast of equal flavor (samara-sa) with the hosts of Heruka’s goddesses and heroes, who possess many flavors and are free from anger and illusion;
it is the yogic mind situated in the lotus, born of supreme delight, and having the nature of moonlight.
Having played with that which is the singular essence of power, consisting of innate bliss, and having the nature of all Buddhas. || 727 ||
Vajragarbha, in a secluded place, with the supreme joy of meditative equipoise, one should perform the *heruka* rites;
the assembly of goddesses together with the heroes, free from the impurities of various corpses and essences through illusion,
their minds joined upon the lotus, arising in supreme bliss, are of the nature of moonlight.
The essence of the innate nature, which is solely attached to play, is the reality of all Buddhas. 727.
The Heroic Protector, together with Ānanda, has definitively taught the characteristics of the fourth [empowerment];
that is the essence of Saṃvara, the omniscient nature along with the three stages.
One should bestow the remaining observances and so forth; whatever is hidden in Saṃvara, one should make the mind blissful.
The yoginī should definitively teach the secret characteristics through the symbolic indications of the heart-essence of the tantra. 728.
If you do not know the characteristic of the yogic mind from the basis of Cakrasaṃvara, what is the purpose of the assembly of yoginīs? What is the purpose of teaching it to sentient beings? (729)
Endowed with these points, the fourfold empowerment is taught exactly as it was explained in the glorious Cakrasaṃvara Tantra. 730.
Likewise, it is said:
"The vase empowerment is the first; the second is the secret empowerment.
The third is the wisdom-knowledge empowerment; the fourth is likewise thereafter. (731)
From the glorious *Guhyasamāja-tantra*, the nature of which is characterized by supreme joy,
the well-praised siddhi is taught as non-abiding coemergence (*sahaja*).
In the glorious *Cakrasaṃvara-tantra*, the coemergent mind is first elaborated.
One possessed of intelligence should understand through the explicit indication of signs. 732.
The yogi is always present within saṃsāra as innate joy;
in that very state, the various rituals of mantra and mudrā are taught as being innate. 733.
Those who do not understand the teaching on the joy expressed as the coemergent Heruka are outside the cycle of Cakrasaṃvara;
for them, spiritual accomplishment is very far away. 734.
That which is the supreme bliss at all times is what he called "the assembly" (gaṇa). Both the assembly and supreme bliss abide as dependent origination. 735.
"Assembly" is taught as the ritual method; from that arises Cakrasaṃvara.
Thus, the assembly is called Saṃvara, and all of that is expressed as Heruka. 736 ||
He who is the coemergent Cakrasaṃvara, the beginningless Buddha; whose various forms are emanated through the ritual of self-awareness;
this glorious one, not born from causes, who is joined with the vajra and lotus—together with Heruka, he has become the Protector. 737.
In the *Sarvaguṇālaṃkāratantrodaya*, this meaning was well-spoken: "The glorious Heruka, when properly practiced, is the accomplisher of all desired aims. (738)
That which is known as the "limb of the other" is the disciple who has received empowerment;
that very thing is known among all yoginīs as the "innate limb. 739.
He who desires to attain realization from elsewhere while [ignoring] the six mudrās, which consist of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), is a partaker of suffering. (740)
Having abandoned this mudrā of the limbs, which is innate and formless, whoever desires perfect knowledge elsewhere is destined for suffering. 740
Having taken hold of the essence of beings according to one's capacity and through the prescribed rite, one should teach them innate bliss, which is the supreme essence of practice. 741.
What is the ritual of passion? From the *Saṃvara*, it is the grasping of sentient beings;
coemergent joy is emptiness, which is supreme within saṃsāra. 741.
Thus it was said:
"All the Vajra Lords have minds whose true nature is the reality of passion."
They bring about the awakening born of passion, which seeks the welfare of all sentient beings. || 742 ||
All the Vajra Lords, contemplating the meaning of that very passion, shall realize enlightenment born from passion for the benefit of all sentient beings. 742.
Therefore, my mantra-practitioner who seeks awakening should perform all physical, vocal, and mental activities according to the prescribed rule, for that is considered the path to awakening. (743)
The mantrin who has realized this meaning should perform the ritual actions with a mind that understands all [phenomena] as body, speech, and mind. 743.
This constant protection for you is the commitment of the perfected ones' samaya; it is declared by all the Buddhas to be equal [to them], the supreme command of the Sovereign Mistress. (744)
This vow of the accomplished samaya must always be guarded;
it has been well-spoken by all the Buddhas. This supreme permission is now examined. 744.
As it was said:
"Enough with this extensive discourse for those who speak mantras."
This is to be accomplished specifically through the mind, for from the mind arises perfect awakening. || 745 ||
The extensive manifestation of many results is taught by the proponents of Secret Mantra:
through the distinction of mental accomplishment, perfect enlightenment arises from the mind. (745)
Thus it has been said:
"That which is the fruit, the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), is the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha."
Herukavajra is the very embodiment of the *samaya*, manifest as the Dharma-body and the Enjoyment-body. || 746 ||
Whatever is the fruit of the bodhicitta, that is the supreme primordial wisdom of the Buddha; this Vajra Heruka will manifest as the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya. 746.
Having gathered the manifold supreme splendor of the heroic yoginī,
one should thereafter satisfy the innate form by means of the recitation of the mantra.
The yoginīs of the sense faculties, their minds delighted by the supreme variety of forms, having attained coemergence, are supremely intent upon the recitation of secret mantra. 747.
Having worshipped [it] in its innate form (sahajarūpa), one should dismiss it;
for one who seeks the ultimate reality (tattvārthin), one should cast a small amount of the pigment into a great river. || 748 ||
Having made excellent offerings to the sahaja-form of the colored powders, request them to depart.
After giving away even a small portion of the colored powders for the sake of others, cast them into a great river or similar body of water. 748.
Thereafter, at midnight, the wise one should perform the worship of the six heroic goddesses in that very place, preceded by the consumption of the sacrificial porridge (caru).
Then, at midnight, the wise hero, having first partaken of the offerings and food, should perform worship according to the tantra itself. 749.
Having arrived at the site of the mandala ground, one should worship the Guru with the offerings of the five desires, both external and internal. (750)
Having arrived at the site of the mandala ground, one should worship the guru;
endowed with both the outer and the inner, one partakes of the five objects of desire. 750.
As is Heruka, so is the Goddess and likewise the Guru; the fruit resulting from the worship of Heruka, the Goddess, and the Guru is identical. (751)
Just as with Heruka, so it is with the goddess; and the guru is likewise.
The fruit of making offerings to Heruka, the goddess, and the guru is the same. 751.
Then one should give to the guru the teacher’s fee as spoken by the Tathāgata,
having offered a hundred thousand pieces of gold and various kinds of jewels.
Then, one should offer to the Guru the offerings spoken of by the Tathāgata: the offering of hundreds of thousands of gold pieces, and various kinds of precious gems. 752.
A hundred pairs of garments, as well as elephants, horses, and a kingdom;
earrings, bracelets, necklaces, and excellent finger-rings. (753)
Wealth consisting of pairs numbering one hundred, elephants, horses, and kingdoms;
earrings, bracelets, necklaces, and excellent finger-rings. 753.
Having prostrated, one should announce [the request] to one who wears the sacred thread, a golden [image], one's own wife, or even a daughter, or a male or female servant, or a sister. (754)
One should offer the supreme golden vessel after having prostrated to one's own wife, daughters, male and female servants, and female attendants. 754.
The wise one should offer himself to the guru with his whole being:
"From this day forward, I am your slave; I have surrendered myself to you. (755)
With the self-nature of all things, the wise one should offer [himself] as a supreme gift; from this day forward, I have offered myself to you as your slave. (755)
When the practitioner has performed this according to the rules with certainty, the ḍākinīs and the Mothers of Yoga are pleased with him. (756)
Having performed that ritual in such a manner, the practitioner becomes utterly certain;
thereafter, there is the union with that very ḍākinī. 756.
The Ḍākinīs, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī—these, together with the Ḍākinīs, roam throughout the entire world along with the practitioner (sādhaka). 757.
Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī—these move about in the world together with the ḍākinīs and the practitioners (sādhakas). 757.
All the servants of that practitioner [obey him], there is no doubt;
they shall attain yogic perfection, and the three worlds will be unimpeded for them. (758)
The practitioner has no doubt that all [beings] will be like his servants;
once this application is accomplished, he cannot be turned back by the three worlds. 758.
"Assuming the form of the Teacher, I accept worship with diligence;
this is the meaning I have declared: the worship of the Guru must be performed. (759)
The Master, dwelling within the body, accepts offerings through diligent effort;
I have clearly taught this meaning: one should perform worship to the Guru. 759
Having performed worship with one's entire being toward Heruka and the others in the Saṃvara [mandala], the wise practitioner should then engage in the conduct according to his capacity. 760.
Having perfectly completed the excellent worship of Hevajra, Cakrasaṃvara, and others with all material offerings, the wise one should thereafter engage in the conduct. 760.
The Ritual for Consecration. || o || End of Chapter 17.
This is the ritual for empowerment. Closer 17.

Alternatively, in the place of one's own mental preference, one who is joined with the yoga of the nature of the wheel should perform the entire ritual procedure for the purpose of consecration within the mind-made wheel of Heruka. 761.
Alternatively, for the sake of empowerment, one who possesses the yoga of the nature of the wheel should perform all the rituals in a delightful mandala that is a source of joy for the mind. 761.
The mantra-practitioner, endowed with the previously mentioned yoga, adorned with the true reality, and following the aforementioned ritual procedure,
should offer [the oblation].
The consecration [should be performed] for such a disciple. || 762 ||
The mantrin endowed with yoga, as previously taught, should bestow empowerment upon a disciple such as this, following the ritual for the adornment of excellent food as previously explained. 762.
But the yogin situated there [should visualize the deity] joined with the left [consort], who is between Vīra and Ādyā, according to the procedure for the practice of the Left Way (vāmācāra).
One should not give everything that is most beautiful. || 763 ||
In that place, the yogi is endowed with the first hero at the center and on the left;
through the conduct of the left, he constantly bestows all that is most beautiful. 763.
Having explained the four joys according to the ritual procedure, which is well-guarded and secret, show compassion for the tantra; [practice] power, vigor, and co-emergent conduct. 764.
The ritual of the four joys, which are thoroughly concealed within the continuum, has been well taught;
now explain how the power of compassion abides perfectly as the coemergent. 764.
In the center of the lotus, upon the excellent nose,
is the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), which has the nature of the entire world and the form of the Ocean of Milk, arisen from the vajra.
Know that the glorious Saṃvara is always flowing. || 765 ||

Within the lotus, at the tip of the supreme nose, there is the form of a milk ocean born from the vajra; it is a wish-fulfilling jewel, the nature of all beings, wherein the glorious Cakrasaṃvara, the awareness, flows perpetually. 765.

He knows the protection wheel, the offering, the auspicious opening of the casket, the extraction of the mantra, as well as the protection, the forceful mandala practice, and the ritual accomplishment. || 766 ||

The ritual of the *bali* offering, the protection wheel, the excellent liberation from the *kha-sbyor*, the extraction of mantras, as well as the protection, eloquence, and the *sādhana* of the mandala. 766.
When endowed with these seven, he is ordained as an Ācārya;
prosperity rests in his hands, effectively accomplishing all desires.
All of these are perfectly endowed; the master shall explain them.
The glory that has come into his hands bestows all desires. 767.
For those disciples in this tantra who have been consecrated in the glorious *Samāja-tantra* and have mastered the seven secrets that are to be kept hidden.
In that very same way, the Guru should explain those [mudrās]. || 768 ||
"In the glorious *Guhyasamāja Tantra*, it is taught that the empowerment hidden within the truth is to be conferred by the guru upon the disciple at all times. (768)
The procedure for initiation devoid of the outer mandala. || 18 ||
This is the ritual for those who wish to receive empowerment in the outer maṇḍala. Closer 18.
This dharma is well-established, pure and free from affliction from the very beginning;
it is joined with all mandalas and beautifully adorned in every form. || 769 ||
This ritual for perfect consecration is primordially pure and faultless; it is perfectly endowed with all maṇḍalas and beautifully adorned in every respect. 769.
Since the world arises from the mind and is characterized by innate bliss, the wise person does not establish [reality] in any way whatsoever. (770)
Since all wandering beings arise from the mind and possess the characteristic of being co-emergent, therefore, O one of noble intelligence, perform the consecration in every location. (770)
The consecration of both images and books is said to pertain to worldly matters;
relying upon worldly convention, the wise perform the rite of consecration. (771)
It is taught that the consecration of images and books is for the sake of the world; relying upon worldly convention, the wise should perform the consecration. 771.
Regarding the accomplishment of the pill of the *upahṛdaya*, its consecration for the objective has been taught;
having reflected upon this, the excellent minister—
One should perform the consecration in brief. || 772 ||
It is taught that one should especially abide in the domain of that which is accomplished through the *gandha* (fragrant paste) of the *upahr̥daya* (near-heart mantra).
Having traveled there, the excellent practitioner should perform the concise consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). 772.
Placing the drinking of Soma at the forefront, adorned with all ornaments and protected by heroic guards, he set out upon the path.
Having first partaken of the lunar draught, adorned with every ornament, and being perfectly endowed with the hero’s protection, he stands well-established upon the path of entry. 773.
Having recited the *āli* and *kāli*, one should cause the deities to dwell [therein];
by that means, one should consecrate everything, such as images, books, and so forth. (774)
Having recited the *ālikālī* verses well, one should perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the deities;
all [images] such as cast metal statues and books should likewise be thoroughly consecrated. 774.

The wise one should bathe the deities with the consecrated victory-vessel (vijayakumbha),
and then he should also sprinkle them with another vessel containing the water of accomplishment (siddhi).
The wise one should perform the bathing of the deity through the recitation over the Victory Vase (vijaya-kalaśa).
Then, with another vase, he should confer empowerment for the sake of attaining siddhi. 776.
The practitioner of gentle yoga who possesses such characteristics as these performs everything according to the prescribed rite, as it is approved in the tantra. (777)
The minor yoga is Vajrasattva; such is its defining characteristic. One should perform all the ritual procedures exactly as they are taught in the tantra. 777.
The middling rite should be performed by means of meditative concentration;
for everything that has been stated by the speaker of truth regarding the installation [of the image], it is to be done in this middling manner. || 778 ||
"By means of the intermediate application for the deceased, one should perform the intermediate rites for the support;
whatever is taught regarding consecration and so forth, that has been thus explained. (778)
The hero, whose self is endowed with innate bliss and whose mind is unshakable, being possessed of supreme qualities, should practice by means of mind-only. || 779 ||
I am Sahaja-Ānanda; the mind of the Hero is unshakable.
Possessing the qualities of greatness, I practice the state of Mind-Only in all things. 779
In a single instant, indeed, everything becomes firmly established;
endowed with the excellence of all aspects, they are honored by all the Buddhas. (780)
In an instant, everything became firmly established; it was endowed with the excellence of all aspects and praised by all the perfect Buddhas. 780.
[eyeskip] Furthermore, the Great Yoga is characterized by non-duality;
it is the foundation of all glorious wheels, arisen from the self-arisen Cakrasaṃvara. 781 ||
The yogin who has become fourfold, possessing the characteristics of the four joys and the four characteristics, perfectly worships all the Buddhas. 782.
Accompanied by laughter, dance, and other festivities, one should perform the drinking of soma and other rites;
at night, there should be a great festival there together with the heroes and the lords of heroes.
One should partake of the lunar drink and so forth; endowed with laughter, grace, and the like, there, in the great joy of the night, the hero and the mistress of heroes abide. 783.
Relying upon the *Samāja* and other tantras,
the wise one always performs the entire supreme rite of consecration by means of a counter-clockwise rotation.

Having properly relied upon the assembly and so forth, the wise one should always perform everything with the left side turned toward [the deity], according to the supreme ritual for consecration. 784.
The Ritual for Consecration. || o || End of Chapter 19.
This is the ritual for consecration. [End of Chapter] 19.
One should draw the great wheel of the Śrīsaṃvara within the Saṃvara [mandala];
through the yoga of the form of Saṃvara, by means of its retention, it becomes Saṃvara. (785)
The glorious Great Cakrasaṃvara, through a union such as that of Saṃvara, will become Saṃvara when held. 785.

O wise one, having written the excellent King of Mantras in the form of the letter *E* in the center upon birch bark (*bhūrja*) according to the ritual using saffron, sandalwood, and other substances, [this] indeed belongs to the illustrious Haṃsa;
it destroys all calamities, brings victory, and when bound upon the arms, it is always auspicious.
It bestows success when recited according to the ritual procedure for cow's urine as prescribed in various mantras. || 786 ||
In the center of such [a mandala], the glorious and wise one should write the king of secret mantras.
With camphor, saffron, sandalwood, and so forth, the glorious and faithful king himself—
always bound upon the excellent banner that conquers all harm and brings victory— should be arrayed.
Reciting various secret mantras and performing rituals, they bestow the accomplishments (siddhis). 786 ||
One should write it ending with *svāhā* for pacification (*śānti*) and with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*);
for subjugation (*vaśya*), it is joined with the syllable *hoḥ*, and for killing (*māraṇa*), it is joined with *hūṃ phaṭ*. || 787 ||
For pacifying, write "svāhā" at the end; for enriching, [write] "namas"; for magnetizing, it is correctly endowed with "hoḥ"; for slaying, one should apply "hūṃ phaṭ. (787)
For those who strive for the welfare of sentient beings without knowing the Heruka yoga, their labor in discourse will not result in the welfare of sentient beings. (788)

If one does not know how to apply the *he ru ka* [union], though one abides striving for the benefit of sentient beings, that weariness and exhaustion will not result in the welfare of sentient beings. (788)
The means of accomplishment, the bali offering and homa, the consecration, and likewise the mandala—endowed with all of these is the characteristic of Herukāṅga. (789)
The sādhana, the torma offering, the fire ritual, the consecration, and likewise the mandala—all these are perfectly endowed with the characteristics of the glorious Heruka’s body. 789.
Having resided at the glorious Ratnagiri for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, this *maṇḍalopāyikā* was composed by the wise master Bhūvācārya. (790)
Dwelling on the glorious Jewel Mountain, for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, the master Vimalamati has composed this method of the maṇḍala. 790.
The *Maṇḍalopāyikā* named *Śrīsaṃvarodaya* is completed. || o ||
The ritual of the Cakrasaṃvara maṇḍala is complete.

In the year [blank], on the fourth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Caitra, during the victorious reign of the illustrious Baladeva—the supreme sovereign (paramabhaṭṭāraka), the lord of lords (rājādhirāja)—this manuscript was written.

It belongs to the Śākya monk Sādhuśrīdeva at the illustrious Mānadeva Mahāvihāra. Whoever recites it, even if burdened by great sins, shall attain the fruit of the Unsurpassed (anuttara-phala) in this very life. Om.
